# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

insights.line: What would make it clearly worth it?

whys.g1: The three answers are about different things (trying a pair at a matinee first, picking up audience questions in a big hall, and an end-seat workaround), so leaving each on its own is how I'd sort them, and there are no group names to be vague.
whys.g2: Tomás's end-seat answer doesn't say what would make it worth it, but it was left on its own rather than put in a group, and nothing junk or explicit was grouped.

founder.order_why: The look-back window (screen 4) is wedged between two context screens that carry the same heading, so the context step is split around it rather than finished first; the rest flows from context to problem to solution to sending.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 show the same kicker and question ('Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies.'), so the context reads as asked twice.
founder.missing: Nothing about money: no screen asks my price ($599 glasses, $20/month Pro), who pays (the wearer, HSA/FSA eligible), or what they spend today on captioning apps and hearing-aid extras. There is also no commitment step to test, such as ordering the caption glasses with free returns. Screen 4 also has a typo, 'aduts'.

PRIMARY.order_why: It goes from whether I talk with hearing people, to a recent time I lost the thread, to the idea, then whether I'd wear it, which follows the way I'd think it through.
PRIMARY.asked_twice: Screens 4 and 5 both send me back to my last conversation to judge captions for it, and screen 5 calls AirCaps an app while screen 6 says glasses, so it felt like the same question twice with the thing itself unclear.
PRIMARY.missing: Nothing asked what I already do when I lose the conversation, like lipreading, asking people to repeat, hearing aids, a phone caption app like Live Transcribe, or bringing an interpreter. Nothing asked where it happened or how noisy it was, how often it happens, or what I'd pay.

screens.why7: The card wants 1 to 4 benefits, each at most 9 words, naming what changes compared with today's way, with an "I'm not sure" escape; my row is nine words, a noun phrase against today's way, one gain, and the escape is there.
screens.instead: What does it do better than the way they get by today (lipreading, hearing aids, phone captions)? One a line, up to four, e.g. "fewer times asking people to repeat".

screens.why1: Straight after I typed what AirCaps does better than today's way, it makes sense to see Keel's tidied version of that benefit and the belief it will test.
screens.why2: "More of the talk followed without asking for repeats" is a stiff noun pile I'd need to reread; I'd say "following more without asking people to repeat", and the intro's "they name the gain in their own words" doesn't match a stranger answering a fixed better-or-not scale.
screens.why3: Asking people to repeat themselves, or nodding along at the table, is exactly what my users and my co-founder live every week, so I can judge this row from inside it.
screens.why4: One row holding the one benefit I lead with, not bundled or split, and the add/remove room lets me add a second, such as keeping eye contact instead of staring at a phone.
screens.why5: It still means what I typed ("Following more without asking anyone to repeat"), and nothing of AirCaps or the glasses leaks into the stranger-facing hard case.
screens.why7: The row is a noun phrase saying what changes against today's way, the belief carries my one kept benefit, and the case is the study's problem clause ("the last time they lost the conversation with hearing people"), not any last occasion, so a "no difference" or "worse" against the 1-in-3 bar can refute it.
screens.instead: Row: "Following more without asking people to repeat"; belief: "For most, the last time they lost the conversation with hearing people, it would have let them follow more without asking anyone to repeat."

screens.why1: Right after what it does better, it is natural to ask what it costs the wearer in effort to start, which closes the solution step.
screens.why2: 'What will they have to do to start using it?' with 'setup, extra steps or learning' is plain to me, and I answered it in my own words without a second read.
screens.why3: I know exactly what a wearer has to do (put the glasses on in conversations, charge them nightly, pair to the phone), so this is squarely my product and my customers' days.
screens.why4: The only chip is the escape 'I'm not sure', which fits a typed list where I might not know the efforts, and the four-row, nine-word limit suits my two short efforts.
screens.why5: Nothing is rewritten here; my two efforts stand as I typed them, and the frame 'Solution · 4 of 4' adds no meaning of its own.
screens.why7: Both rows are steps the wearer takes themselves, base-form, in their voice, under nine words and distinct; charging daily is the new habit the card asks for, and neither repeats Compatibility's phone-online row or Purchase friction.
screens.instead: What will they have to do to start using it, and keep doing day to day? (setup, new habits or learning; up to four, each up to 9 words)

screens.why1: Right after I said what they'd have to do to start, it's obvious Keel shows me the efforts it drafted so I can check them before picking one to test.
screens.why2: Wearing the caption glasses in conversations and charging them every day are exactly how I'd say it to my own users; nothing needs a second read.
screens.why3: Both are things a deaf or hard-of-hearing wearer does themselves every week, and they would know at once whether they'd do it.
screens.why4: Two distinct efforts, one habit of wear and one daily chore, both in plain words with no overlap; the repeated title in the intro is only cosmetic.
screens.why5: The wear row keeps what I typed as revised, and the daily charge is a true cost of our hardware; neither leaks anything wrong, though pairing to the phone is no longer on the list.
screens.why7: Each row is one base-form effort of at most 9 words in 'their' voice that the wearer takes themselves, not a sign-off, a purchase step or a Compatibility condition, and 1 to 4 rows are within the count, so a yes or a no could answer either belief.
screens.instead: Add 'Pair the glasses with the app on their phone' as the one-time setup, beside 'Wear the caption glasses in conversations' and 'Charge the glasses every day'.

screens.why1: After I listed what it takes to start using AirCaps, the next step is to pick which effort is most likely to stop people, and that is clearly why the screen is here.
screens.why2: Wearing the caption glasses and charging them every day are plain words for me and for the deaf and hard-of-hearing people I sell to.
screens.why3: Both are things the wearer does themselves, and they would know at once whether they would do them.
screens.why4: Two distinct efforts: wearing the glasses in conversation and charging them daily, with no overlap and nothing I would call missing.
screens.why5: My row is kept word for word and picked, and nothing from my product or team leaks into the belief.
screens.why7: Both rows are efforts the wearer takes themselves, on the one measure, and the belief can be supported or refuted, but 'Charge the glasses every day' is not in my list, so it reads as Keel's added habit step with no label and no reason beside it, which the card requires.
screens.instead: Same list, but with the second row marked as Keel's suggestion and its reason: Charge the glasses every day (Keel's suggestion: a daily charge is the new habit all-day captioning asks, and a flat battery mid-dinner ends the captions).

screens.why1: Right before the study goes out, deciding whether to collect emails from people who want to try the glasses is exactly the step I'd expect, and it matches my 15-day risk-free returns commitment.
screens.why2: 'Pilot' is plain startup language to me as a founder, and the hint spells out exactly what respondents will see and where I'll find the yeses.
screens.why3: Whether I want a list of deaf and hard-of-hearing people ready to try AirCaps is my own call, answerable at once.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it, the two are distinct, and no escape chip is needed for a founder's own setting.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or roles is reworded here, and the respondent line 'Would you try this for real?' leaks no product name or role.

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the questions belongs in the last step before the link goes out, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: The question, the two names and the credit cost read plainly on first pass, and the hint answers my first worry by saying every question is also written on screen with type or tap answers.
screens.why3: My respondents mostly won't hear the voice, so what I can actually judge is the face, how clearly lips read on video, and whether text leads; a 5-second audio sample is something I and many of them can only half judge.
screens.why4: Two voices with audio previews leave out what matters most for deaf and hard-of-hearing people: a look at each face for lipreading, and a text-first or captioned-video choice.
screens.why5: My segment's words are kept in the question, nothing about AirCaps or the glasses leaks into the interviewer choice, and my pick of the preselected face stands.
screens.instead: Who should ask deaf or hard-of-hearing adults your questions? Each question appears as large text first, with the interviewer's face and captions below it: Daphne (see her face and captions, 5 s) / Saskia (see her face and captions, 5 s) / Text only, no video

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks the questions, it's natural to choose how my deaf and hard-of-hearing respondents answer before the study goes out.
screens.why2: Read, tap, type, talk and pick are plain words for me and my users, and the Daphne option says the questions are also written on screen.
screens.why3: I know how my people take in a question: most read text easily, many prefer it to audio, and some don't speak at all, so I can answer this from what I know.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct and cover my real choice, Read and tap, and typing is offered on both, so non-speaking signers like the ASL instructor aren't shut out, though a sign-language answer mode is absent.
screens.why5: My pick of Read and tap stands as typed, and nothing about the glasses or captions leaks into how respondents answer.
screens.instead: AI interviewer · Daphne: every question is captioned on screen as Daphne asks it on video; they answer by typing, tapping or talking (lead with the captions for a deaf audience).

screens.why1: Once the interviews are set up, the obvious last step is deciding who gets the link, so this sits right where I'd expect it at the end of the flow.
screens.why2: The three choices are in plain founder words (people I know, people from a search, one open link for a group), and I understand each on first read.
screens.why3: I know exactly who I can reach: deaf and hard-of-hearing people I've met through TranscribeGlass, the waitlist and testers, so I can answer this from my own situation.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover how I'd reach people, but the second option mentions a 'Contacts page' I haven't seen in this flow, and the third says nothing about whether an open link posted in a Deaf community group can be screened to the segment.
screens.why5: Nothing about my product or study wording is changed here; it is only about distribution, and my pick of people I know by name is kept.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? -- People I know by name (I send each their own link) / People from a Keel search (pick a list from your contacts; Keel makes a link each) / One open link for a group (post it where they gather, like a hard-of-hearing forum; each person signs in with Google)

screens.why_b1: The stage verdict 'Holding up' sits under the title, the tally says 3 of 3 beliefs hold, and each card gives its own count against its bar (7 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7), so I can see why the page holds.
screens.why_b2: Each card's status line says what was counted ('said yes, easily or most of the time', 'would do it'), over 7 people, and where the bar sits (5 of 7), so all three read on first look.
screens.why_b3: The three dimension names are mine and the beliefs are recognisable, but Keel's solution statement is garbled ('wearing the glasses the app on lightweight glasses shows... and gets back live captions... inside the lens'), and the relative-advantage line ('would have given them more of the talk followed') is mangled grammar rather than my words.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the page says what a unanimous solution stage means for AirCaps: no line about moving on to the commercial question, and nothing about the 3 who would wear the glasses only on a condition; 'What it measures' explains the method, not the next step.
screens.why_b5: The 7 respondents stay visible on every line and the 3 conditional wearers are flagged, but 7 of 7 'a lot' from seven people is presented with no word that seven is a small sample, which reads softly stronger than the data carries.
screens.instead: Holding up, all three beliefs at 7 of 7 against a bar of 5, but only seven people answered, and 3 of them would wear the glasses only on a condition. Open Adoption friction to see what the condition is, then check whether Commercial holds before ordering stock; and fix the statement to say 'the glasses show live captions of what the people nearby are saying, inside the lens'.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside its deciding number, '7 of 7 said yes, easily or most of the time · bar 5 of 7', so I know it held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts four answer choices over 7 people, labelled for and against, and the strip marks my bar at 5 of 7, all readable on first look.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility and 'could read captions while watching faces' are the condition I picked on the way in, in my words.
screens.why_b4: The So line tells me concretely that reading captions while watching faces won't stop my wearers, and sends me to adoption friction as the real obstacle.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible and the count line calls it 'a lean, not a call', but the So line then says flatly that this 'is not what will stop them', which is firmer than seven hypothetical answers can carry.
screens.instead: From these 7, reading captions while watching faces doesn't look like the blocker (a lean, not a call); adoption friction, below, looks more likely to be.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 7 of 7 said better against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know the verdict and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts 'better' over the 7 who answered, and the strip puts my bar at 5, though 'Better · 7 7 a lot' stutters a little.
screens.why_b3: Relative advantage and 'more of the talk followed without asking for repeats', after the time they lost the conversation with hearing people, is my benefit and my problem in my words.
screens.why_b4: 'All 7 imagined it going better' plus a pointer to Adoption friction tells me where to look next, but not what this means for AirCaps, such as whether to lead with this benefit in the pitch.
screens.why_b5: The low n is flagged as a lean, but the asked line shows people judged 'AirCaps, an app' on any recent conversation rather than caption glasses on the time they lost the thread, so the card claims more about my belief than that question can carry.
screens.instead: Ask 'Think of the most recent time you lost the conversation with hearing people. Would AirCaps, caption glasses, have done that better for you?' and then say: 7 of 7, all a lot, a lean on 7 people, so lead the pitch with following without asking for repeats and check Adoption friction next.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside the deciding number, '7 of 7 would do it · bar 5 of 7', so I know it held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The bars plainly count Yes 4, the condition 3 and 0 against over 7 people, and the strip puts my bar at 5 of 7, all clear on first look.
screens.why_b3: 'Adoption friction' and 'Most would wear the caption glasses in conversations' are the dimension and effort I picked, in my words.
screens.why_b4: The So line only restates the 4-and-3 split and points 'below' for what would make it worth it, but it never says the real next step: the catch is the look on the face, so test the frames' look and offer a try-before-you-buy.
screens.why_b5: n and 'a lean, not a call' are honest, but the So line promises that what follows explains the three conditions, and only Harriet's matinee trial bears on that; Ruth's quote is about audience pickup and Tomás's about his end-seat workaround.
screens.instead: Holding up, 7 of 7, a small lean; the catch for 3 of 7 is the look, so show the frames on real faces and offer a borrow-a-pair trial like Harriet asks for.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Holding up' and 'held, 7 of 7' sit right beside the bar of 5 of 7, so I know the verdict and the number behind it.
screens.why_b3: 'Most would wear the caption glasses in conversations' is the adoption-friction line I checked, worded as revision 24 set it.
screens.why_b4: Nothing says what to do next, even though Harriet's quote clearly points to a try-before-you-buy demo and Ruth's points to audience-mic pickup in large halls.
screens.why_b5: All three quotes are filed under 'Only if it looks ordinary on my face', a condition none of them states, and a dangling 'for' follows each one; the n of 7 also goes unremarked.
screens.why_b6: The quotes teach me things I did not type: reading the lens under stage lights, catching audience questions in a big hall, and a one-sided-deafness seating workaround that competes with the glasses. But the single repeated theme label is noise, not a theme.
screens.instead: Give each conditional yes its own theme: 'let me try a pair at a show first' (Harriet), 'catch the audience, not just the stage' (Ruth), and 'my seating trick mostly works' (Tomás, a competing workaround). Drop the stray 'for', and say what to try next: a loaner or demo pair, and room-wide pickup.

screens.why1: As the first screen, it makes sense to check that I actually talk with hearing people before asking anything else, and that is my whole life at work, at the shop and at the theatre.
screens.why2: "Hearing people" is how I and every deaf person I know say it, so I can answer it straight away.
screens.why3: I know without guessing whether I talked with hearing people this week, because I do almost every day.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it with nothing missing, and a gate question needs no escape, so leaving one out is right.
screens.why5: It uses the segment's own words and gives nothing away about any product or what the study is selling.
screens.why6: It is short and easy to say, though "I'll read two options" before a plain yes-or-no is a bit stiff when §17 says the screener just ends with "Yes or no."
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you talk face to face with a hearing person? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after confirming I talk with hearing people every week, asking whether I actually got lost in one this past week is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: I'd say 'lost track of' rather than 'lost the conversation', but I understand it on first hearing; it's how deaf people talk about dinner tables.
screens.why3: I know exactly whether I got lost at a family dinner or a work lunch this week, so I can answer from my own life.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, and the chips belong to the story box after a Yes, so they aren't the gate's escape.
screens.why5: Nothing of a product leaks, but 'at a table' narrows the founder's face-to-face conversation, so someone who got lost standing in a meeting or a shop has to say No.
screens.why6: One short question ending 'Yes or no.' is easy to hold, though as a deaf listener I'd rely on the on-screen card rather than the voice.
screens.why7: Two fixed answers in order, no escape, the window named, and the event is the part that hurts (losing the thread), not the routine of talking with hearing people, so a No is truly possible for someone who followed fine this week.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you lose track of a conversation with hearing people? Yes · No

screens.why1: After asking whether I lost the thread at a table with hearing people last week, showing me a captioning idea for exactly that moment is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Live captions, glasses and eye contact are things I deal with all the time, so I get it on first read, though 'you wear your lightweight glasses' reads oddly, as if I already own a pair.
screens.why3: Reading captions while trying to keep looking at the person talking is my everyday problem, so I can judge this from my own life.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options shown.
screens.why5: It is presented openly as an idea to imagine, in words I would use, and nothing about who the company sells to or their own labels for people comes through.
screens.why6: The second and third sentences repeat 'lightweight glasses' and 'live captions inside the lens' from the first, so heard aloud it is four sentences that say the same thing twice, a mouthful before any question.
screens.instead: Imagine AirCaps, an app on lightweight glasses that shows live captions inside the lens. When people near you talk, their words appear in front of your eyes. The people building it believe it would let you read the words while keeping eye contact.

screens.why1: Right after the glasses idea, it makes sense to ask whether I could keep my eyes on faces and still read the words, since that is the whole point for me.
screens.why2: Reading captions and watching faces are my everyday words; I lipread and I use live captions on my phone, so I get it on first hearing.
screens.why3: At my last conversation I had no captions in front of my eyes, so I would be half guessing what I could have done, and 'last conversation' could mean one with my deaf friends rather than the hearing people at the table I was just asked about.
screens.why4: The four ability options run cleanly from easily to no, and I can't tell fits for when I truly don't know.
screens.why5: It only uses what the idea card already showed me, captions I can read while seeing faces, and no company terms slip in.
screens.why6: Short, one question, four short options I can hold, and one escape at the end.
screens.why7: This is an ability with the four ability options in order and I can't tell set apart, and it can go either way: some of us manage glancing between phone captions and faces, others lose the lips every time they look down.
screens.instead: Think of your last conversation with hearing people at a table. Could you have read captions and watched their faces at the same time? Yes, easily; yes, most of the time; only sometimes; or no. Or I can't tell.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the captions-while-watching-faces question, asking whether the glasses would have made it better is the obvious next thing to ask me.
screens.why2: I can answer it, but 'tried to follow and join a face-to-face conversation' is stiff; I'd say 'lost track of what people at the table were saying'.
screens.why3: I talk with hearing people every week and know exactly how my last conversation went, so I can answer this from my own life.
screens.why4: The four answers run from a lot better to worse with no gap or overlap, and 'I can't tell' fits for someone who has never worn caption glasses.
screens.why5: Nothing of the founder's plan leaks, but the stem uses their job phrase word for word instead of my words, and 'AirCaps, an app' drops the glasses the card just showed me.
screens.why6: It is short, one question, four short options I can hold, and one escape said last.
screens.why7: The four fixed answers and the escape are right, but the occasion is any last conversation, which may have gone fine, not the hard case from screen 2 (losing the conversation at a table with hearing people), so a 'No difference' may only mean that conversation was easy.
screens.instead: Think of the last time you lost the conversation at a table with hearing people. Would AirCaps, captions inside your glasses, have made that better for you, or not? A lot better · A little better · No difference · Worse · I can't tell

screens.why1: After being shown the glasses and asked if they'd beat what I do now, asking whether I'd actually put them on in conversations is the obvious next thing to ask.
screens.why2: Wearing caption glasses in a conversation is plain to me; I read captions all the time and I'd answer this on first hearing.
screens.why3: Whether I'd wear something on my face at a table with hearing people is my own call, about my own week.
screens.why4: Yes, a real catch, probably not, no, and can't tell cover it, and the catch is the one I'd actually have, not wanting to look like I'm wearing a gadget.
screens.why5: Caption glasses is just what the card already showed me, in words I'd use myself, and nothing of the company's plan leaks through.
screens.why6: One short question, four short options I can hold, and my becoming your in the spoken version sounds natural.
screens.why7: The effort is mine to take, all options sit on whether I'd take it, two for and two against with the conditional mine and specific, and I can't tell is the one escape apart.

screens.why1: After asking whether I'd wear the caption glasses, asking what would make them worth it to me is a natural last question.
screens.why2: Short and plain, and AirCaps is named instead of a bare 'it', so I don't have to work out what it means.
screens.why3: I lose conversations at tables with hearing people every week, so I know exactly what would have to happen for captions to help me keep up and join in.
screens.why4: Just a box to type in, so there are no options.
screens.why5: It uses the product name already shown on the idea card and adds nothing new from the founder's plan.
screens.why6: One short question with no list or symbols, easy to hear once and answer.
screens.instead: What would the caption glasses have to do at a noisy table for you to keep wearing them?
